questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests runtime extensibility, per-endpoint isolation, and safe hot-reload in a gateway.

## Key Concepts
- Strategy pattern for limiter variants
- Registry for dynamic lookup
- Hot-reload with atomic swaps
- Per-endpoint isolation and concurrency control
- Observability and testing

## Code Example
```javascript
type StrategyName = 'TokenBucket'|'FixedWindow'|'SlidingWindow';
interface RateLimiter { acquire(tokens = 1): boolean; }
class TokenBucket implements RateLimiter { constructor(public capacity, public refill){} acquire(n = 1){ return true; } }
class Registry { private m = new Map<string, RateLimiter>(); get(k){ return this.m.get(k); } set(k, v){ this.m.set(k, v); } }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle clock skew in distributed deployments?
- How would you write tests for hot-reload safety and race conditions?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design extensible, runtime-modifiable tooling using common patterns.

## Key Concepts
- Command pattern, Registry, Factory, dynamic imports, plugin isolation
- Runtime extension without recompilation, error handling, help aggregation

## Code Example
```typescript
// Minimal interfaces
interface Command { execute(args: string[]): Promise<void> }
interface CommandFactory { create(): Command }
class CommandRegistry { register(name: string, factory: () => Command); resolve(name: string): Command; list(): string[] }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you sandbox/unload plugins, handle conflicting command names, and security concerns?
- How would you version plugins and roll back faulty ones?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to extend behavior without touching core dispatch logic; demonstrates the Command pattern with a runtime registry.

## Key Concepts
- Command pattern
- Registry-based extensibility
- Safe, non-invasive extension

## Code Example
```javascript
interface Command { execute(args: string[]): void; }
class Registry { private map = new Map<string, Command>(); register(name: string, c: Command) { this.map.set(name, c); } get(name: string): Command | undefined { return this.map.get(name); } }
class Router { constructor(private registry: Registry) {} route(argv: string[]) { const cmd = argv[0]; const command = this.registry.get(cmd); if (command) command.execute(argv.slice(1)); else throw new Error('Unknown command'); } }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle asynchronous commands? 
- How would you ensure thread-safety in a multi-process CLI?

## Why This Is Asked
Real-world fault tolerance requires dynamic policy changes without redeploys. This tests design extensibility, runtime registries, and per-endpoint isolation.

## Key Concepts
- Runtime extensibility and registries
- Pipeline/Chain of Responsibility pattern
- Per-endpoint isolation and non-blocking evaluation
- Metrics and safe error handling

```javascript
interface IPolicy { name: string; configure(params: any): void; onCall(ctx: any, next: () => Promise<any>): Promise<any> }
interface IPolicyFactory { create(config?: any): IPolicy }
class PolicyRegistry { private map = new Map<string, IPolicyFactory>(); register(name: string, f: IPolicyFactory): void; create(name: string, config?: any): IPolicy }
class PolicyPipeline { constructor(policies: IPolicy[]); async execute(ctx: any, fn: ()=> Promise<any>): Promise<any> }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test policy interactions across distributed instances?
- How would you handle policy versioning and backward compatibility?
